fixes.explanation: True! The verse says, "Like a madman shooting firebrands and deadly arrows, so is the man who deceives his neighbor…" Then he says he was only joking. Calling it a joke afterward doesn't un-shoot the arrows. A joke that burns somebody isn't a joke.

It's actually true, friend. The verse says, "Like a madman shooting firebrands and deadly arrows, so is the man who deceives his neighbor…" Then he says he was only joking. The two pictures go together in the same sentence. Saying sorry-just-kidding doesn't pull the arrows back.

Good thinking, but the verse never mentions followers. It says, "Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he become wise in his own eyes." The worry is how the fool sees himself. I bet he'd strut around like the one cookie who thinks he invented the oven.

True! The verse says, "Like cutting off one’s own feet or drinking violence is the sending of a message by the hand of a fool." Sending a message by a fool is put right next to cutting off your own feet. Friend, that's a rough review for a delivery service.
That's right. The verse says, "Like an archer who wounds at random is he who hires a fool or passerby." The one compared to the archer is the one doing the hiring. Wild shots, friend.
Walking along with fools isn't what this verse says, friend. It says, "Like an archer who wounds at random is he who hires a fool or passerby." So it's the hiring that's compared to the archer.

Repeats, yes. The verse says, "As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly." It's a rough picture, friend. He goes back to the same folly again. I once reached for the same hot pan twice in one morning, so I'm not judging.
Hides isn't the word, friend. The verse says, "As a dog returns to its vomit, so a fool repeats his folly." The dog returns, and the fool repeats his folly. The word you're looking for is repeats.
A storm would be a fine thing to announce, but it's not what the slacker says. He says, "A lion is in the road! A fierce lion roams the public square!" The danger he names is a lion, teeth and all.

Not quite, friend, it's the opposite. The verse says, "The slacker buries his hand in the dish; it wearies him to bring it back to his mouth." He's not eating fast. Bringing his hand back to his mouth is what wearies him.

You got it. The verse says, "The slacker is wiser in his own eyes than seven men who answer discreetly." He's measuring himself against seven careful men and coming out ahead. That's a whole lot of confidence for a slacker.
Yes, down deep. The verse says, "The words of a gossip are like choice morsels that go down into the inmost being." The picture is food going down. The place it lands is the inmost being.

Exactly. The verse says, "When he speaks graciously, do not believe him, for seven abominations fill his heart." Gracious words on the outside, seven abominations on the inside. That's a cookie box with a pretty ribbon and nothing good in it.

False is right. The verse says, "Though his hatred is concealed by deception, his wickedness will be exposed in the assembly." His hatred is concealed for now. The verse says his wickedness will be exposed.
That's right. The verse says, "He who digs a pit will fall into it…" The one who digs the pit is the one who falls into it. Dig carefully, friend.
Filling it in isn't what the verse says, friend. It says, "He who digs a pit will fall into it…" Falling into it is the outcome the verse gives. The digger ends up in the pit.

True. The last verse says, "A lying tongue hates those it crushes, and a flattering mouth causes ruin." The flattering mouth sits right beside the lying tongue. We started the chapter with snow in summer, friend, and look where we ended up.
